title: Anticipating Decoder Side-channel Attacks in Fault-tolerant Quantum Computers
authors: Shashvat Shukla, Dan E. Browne, Shin Nishio
abstract: As quantum computing emerges as an applied technology, there is a growing need to protect quantum computers against information security attacks. This work identifies a new class of side-channel attacks against fault-tolerant quantum computers, in which the syndrome data that is sent to the decoder system is used to infer which computation (logical circuit) is taking place on the quantum computer. Our work introduces the concept of gate fingerprints, which describes those patterns present in syndrome data that indicate which logical operation took place on the quantum computer. We show different effects by which logical operations produce gate fingerprints by focusing on Clifford+T computation in the surface code. We then explore how gate fingerprint information can be used to make inferences about the circuits or algorithms run on a quantum computer. Our findings indicate that decoder systems can be a vector for side-channel attacks and thus to prevent this, decoder systems should either be secured or built by a trusted party.
summary: This work details a side-channel attack where an untrusted error correction decoder can deduce the underlying quantum algorithm by analyzing patterns (gate fingerprints) hidden within the syndrome measurement data. The authors demonstrate that these leakage channels exist even in fault-tolerant settings, necessitating that decoder systems be secured or treated as trusted components.
main_problem: The paper identifies a novel side-channel attack vector against fault-tolerant quantum computers where an untrusted decoder can infer the executed logical computation by analyzing syndrome data.
main_result: Distinct logical operations leave detectable statistical patterns, called 'gate fingerprints,' in the spacetime syndrome data processed by the decoder.
method: The analysis formalizes this leakage by defining gate fingerprints as conditional distributions of the spacetime syndrome given a hidden logical gate, using surface code models.
model_or_system: The system modeled is Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computing (FTQC) utilizing surface codes and Clifford+T gates. The attack targets the decoder which processes syndrome measurements derived from stabilizer checks.
key_observables: Spacetime syndrome data, gate fingerprints (statistical patterns in syndrome outcomes), and reconstructed logical gate sequences/ratios over time.
important_parameters: The type of computation (e.g., Amplitude Amplification, HHL) and the level of decoder knowledge (qubit-aware vs. qubit-unaware).
main_assumptions: The decoder is assumed to be correct in its decoding function but untrusted regarding confidentiality; leakage occurs through syndrome data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the threat model flow, show rolling average gate counts for specific algorithms (AA, HHL, QFT), and demonstrate circuit reconstruction via majority voting on repeating patterns.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by formalizing the syndrome leakage setting, defining gate fingerprints using surface code analysis of Clifford+T gates, showing how adversaries combine these fingerprints to infer circuits, and concluding with security recommendations.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, information-theoretic security vulnerability in the control/readout layer of quantum computation, which is highly relevant for anyone designing or simulating large-scale quantum hardware.
analysis_basis: full PDF text, analyzed in chunks

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Threat model for decoder-side confidentiality leakage. The decoder is honest-but-curious, which is assumed to per- form its task of estimating the Pauli frame from the spacetime syndrome, but is not trusted with respect to confidentiality. Even without being given an explicit circuit description, the information available at the decoder interface may be exploited to infer properties of the hidden logical computation, such as the logical gate applied in a given decoding window.

Fig. 3: Gate fingerprint of transversal CX gate on a pair of d = 5 rotated surface code patch. Detector-event probabilities are shown over space and time for the control and target patches. The resulting signature is localized in time but spread over both patches, consistent with the coordinated two-block interaction of the transversal implementation. We set the phys- ical error rates to pidle = 10−3, p1q = 5 × 10−3, p2q = 10−2, preset = 10−3, and pmeas = 10−3.
Fig. 4: Gate fingerprint of lattice surgery-based CX gate. The boundary associated with the XX (ZZ) measurement is high- lighted by a localized increase in detector-event probability.

Fig. 5: Classification metrics for logical gates. H, S, and lattice surgery exhibit distinctive fingerprints and are therefore generally classified correctly, whereas the Pauli gates X, Y , and Z share the same fingerprint under the unbiased Pauli channel, rendering them indistinguishable. 1000 shots per logical gate and 10000 shots for training.
Fig. 6: Rolling mean gate counts of the amplitude amplifica- tion circuit as seen by the decoder.
